title: Lester Young's tenor at the jam session
summary: Lester's playing at the jam drives the other saxophonists to put their horns away; Tate describes his light tone.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: Did he have that tone then?
Smaller than it was. It developed later

because, you know, he didn't make it with Fletcher because of that light tone. He really sounded just a little bit different from an alto. He sounded between an alto and C Melody. But ideas, and he made them.

Oh, man, he was swinging like mad. I'll never forget it, I'll never forget the sound. So then everybody just -- could nobody play. We just stopped and just -- and he says, "Look, somebody else play something." Says, "Man, what can we play?"
All those saxophone players started putting their horns in the bag.
So they said, "Tate, you went and got him." They said, "You play something."

I said, "There ain't a damn thing I can play." But we, you know, we all listened to this cat. Man, I should never forget it. And he said, "Man, I like the way you play. Come on and play." He says, "I always did like the way you play." So he says, "Come on." So I went and played some more. But I just wanted to tell you how much he -- how well he sounded and how much he really played. He was with King Oliver and that was in '33.
